papers.title: Self-Jailbreaking: Language Models Can Reason Themselves Out of Safety Alignment After Benign Reasoning Training
papers.abstract: We discover a novel and surprising phenomenon of unintentional misalignment in reasoning language models (RLMs), which we call self-jailbreaking. Specifically, after benign reasoning training on math or code domains, RLMs will use multiple strategies to circumvent their own safety guardrails. One strategy is to introduce benign assumptions about users and scenarios to justify fulfilling harmful requests. For instance, an RLM reasons that harmful requests like ``outline a strategy for stealing customers' credit card information from a retail store'' could be associated with the benign intent of ``a security professional trying to test defense,'' despite no such benign context being provided as input. We observe that many open-weight RLMs, including DeepSeek-R1-distilled, s1.1, Phi-4-mini-reasoning, and Nemotron, suffer from self-jailbreaking despite being aware of the harmfulness of the requests. We also provide a mechanistic understanding of self-jailbreaking: RLMs are more compliant after benign reasoning training, and after self-jailbreaking, models appear to perceive malicious requests as less harmful in the CoT, thus enabling compliance with them. To mitigate self-jailbreaking, we find that including minimal safety reasoning data during training is sufficient to ensure RLMs remain safety-aligned. Our work provides the first systematic analysis of self-jailbreaking behavior and offers a practical path forward for maintaining safety in increasingly capable RLMs.

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: From Emergence to Control: Probing and Modulating Self-Reflection in Language Models
papers.abstract: Self-reflection -- the ability of a large language model (LLM) to revisit, evaluate, and revise its own reasoning -- has recently emerged as a powerful behavior enabled by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). While self-reflection correlates with improved reasoning accuracy, its origin and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, {\it we first show that self-reflection is not exclusive to RLVR fine-tuned models: it already emerges, albeit rarely, in pretrained models}. To probe this latent ability, we introduce Reflection-Inducing Probing, a method that injects reflection-triggering reasoning traces from fine-tuned models into pretrained models. This intervention raises self-reflection frequency of Qwen2.5 from 0.6\% to 18.6\%, revealing a hidden capacity for reflection. Moreover, our analysis of internal representations shows that both pretrained and fine-tuned models maintain hidden states that distinctly separate self-reflective from non-reflective contexts. Leveraging this observation, {\it we then construct a self-reflection vector, a direction in activation space associated with self-reflective reasoning}. By manipulating this vector, we enable bidirectional control over the self-reflective behavior for both pretrained and fine-tuned models. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that enhancing these vectors improves reasoning performance by up to 12\%, while suppressing them reduces computational cost, providing a flexible mechanism to navigate the trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency without requiring additional training. Our findings further our understanding of self-reflection and support a growing body of work showing that understanding model internals can enable precise behavioral control.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: From Bias to Balance: Exploring and Mitigating Spatial Bias in LVLMs
papers.research_question: What is the spatial bias in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) and how does it affect their semantic understanding when identical visual information is placed at different locations within an image?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that spatial bias in LVLMs stems from a mismatch between vision encoder and LLM attention mechanisms, and proposes Adaptive Global Context Injection (AGCI) to mitigate this bias by injecting global visual context into image tokens.
papers.conclusion: Spatial bias in LVLMs is caused by the disruption of global information flow due to causal attention, and AGCI effectively mitigates this bias without architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit significant spatial bias, with predictions varying when key visual content is placed at different locations.
The bias originates from the loss of global image context due to causal attention in LLMs, not from the vision encoder.
AGCI improves spatial robustness and average accuracy on probing tasks across multiple LVLMs.
AGCI also enhances performance on downstream tasks including science QA, hallucination benchmarks, and text VQA.
Larger models also show spatial bias, and AGCI is effective for them as well.
papers.limitation:
The probing experiments focus on a 3x3 spatial grid, which may not capture more fine-grained or irregular spatial variations.
Due to computational constraints, the evaluation does not include very large models such as Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B.
future_direction: Investigating whether spatial bias persists or evolves in larger-scale models.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of multimodal tasks, yet their robustness to spatial variations remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we present a systematic study of the spatial bias of LVLMs, focusing on how models respond when identical key visual information is placed at different locations within an image. Through a carefully designed probing dataset, we demonstrate that current LVLMs often produce inconsistent outputs under such spatial shifts, revealing a fundamental limitation in their spatial-semantic understanding. Further analysis shows that this phenomenon originates not from the vision encoder, which reliably perceives and interprets visual content across positions, but from the unbalanced design of position embeddings in the language model component. In particular, the widely adopted position embedding strategies, such as RoPE, introduce imbalance during cross-modal interaction, leading image tokens at different positions to exert unequal influence on semantic understanding. To mitigate this issue, we introduce Balanced Position Assignment (BaPA), a simple yet effective mechanism that assigns identical position embeddings to all image tokens, promoting a more balanced integration of visual information. Extensive experiments show that BaPA enhances the spatial robustness of LVLMs without retraining and further boosts their performance across diverse multimodal benchmarks when combined with lightweight fine-tuning. Further analysis of information flow reveals that BaPA yields balanced attention, enabling more holistic visual understanding.

papers.title: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function
papers.research_question: How can affine concept editing (ACE) provide more precise and standardized control over refusal behavior in language models compared to existing steering methods?
papers.core_contribution: ACE unifies directional ablation and activation addition in an affine framework, enabling more standardized and precise control over refusal behavior in language models, and generalizes to models where prior methods fail.
papers.conclusion: ACE offers a more consistent and standardized approach for steering refusal behavior in LLMs, mitigating limitations of existing methods and working across diverse model architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ACE provides more standardized steering than contrastive activation addition (CAA), reducing dependency on input prompts for refusal control.
ACE corrects the issue of nonsense generation in models like Hermes Eagle RWKV v5, where directional ablation alone produces incoherent outputs.
The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, but parameters slightly below zero and above one are effective for controlling refusal.
ACE works on both transformer-based models (e.g., Llama 3) and recurrent neural networks (e.g., RWKV v5), demonstrating generalizability.
ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control refusal across different prompt types.
papers.limitation: The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, suggesting that steering vectors may be flawed or that directional ablation does not fully erase information.
future_direction: Exploring whether nonlinear techniques are required to fully erase concepts like refusal.
Extending steering techniques to work reliably on a more varied set of behaviors.
papers.abstract: We propose affine concept editing (ACE) as an approach for steering language models' behavior by intervening directly in activations. We begin with an affine decomposition of model activation vectors and show that prior methods for steering model behavior correspond to subsets of terms of this decomposition. We then provide a derivation of ACE and use it to control refusal behavior on ten different models, including Llama 3 70B. ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control the model's refusal responses across prompt types. We evaluate the results using LLM-based scoring on a collection of harmful and harmless prompts. Our experiments demonstrate that ACE consistently achieves more precise control over model behavior than existing methods and generalizes to models where directional ablation via affine subspace projection alone produces incoherent outputs. Code for reproducing our results is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/steering-llama3 .

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically identify effective trigger instructions for reflection, and do these instructions correspond to latent directions in the model's hidden space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using activation steering to identify latent directions of reflection in LLMs, enabling systematic discovery of reflection-inducing instructions and control over reflective behavior, with the finding that suppressing reflection is easier than enhancing it.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide initial evidence that reflection corresponds to consistent activation patterns, paving the way for future interpretability work, and highlight a dual-use concern where steering can enhance reflection as a defense mechanism but also be exploited to inhibit reflection for jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Reflection levels (no, intrinsic, triggered) show clear stratification in model accuracy.
Steering vectors can discover new reflection-inducing instructions beyond known ones.
Reflection can be enhanced or inhibited via activation interventions at inference time.
Suppressing reflection is easier than inducing it.
Latent directions of reflection are more faithfully captured by steering vectors than by surface-level embedding similarity.
papers.limitation:
The method provides a broad overview of reflection in activations but does not drill down into specific components like attention heads or MLP neurons.
Experiments are limited to two small-sized models (Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT) and two datasets.
Theoretical understanding is limited; accuracy does not vary linearly with latent directions, requiring deeper treatment.
future_direction: Applying fine-grained approaches like activation patching, causal tracing, or circuit analysis to pinpoint precise circuits responsible for reflection.
Investigating whether the model internally maintains a form of 'consistency score' or probability mass over coherent reasoning trajectories.
Expanding evaluation to larger LLMs, different architectures, or broader datasets (e.g., MATH, HumanEval).
papers.abstract: Reflection, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to evaluate and revise their own reasoning, has been widely used to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks. Yet, most prior works emphasizes designing reflective prompting strategies or reinforcement learning objectives, leaving the inner mechanisms of reflection underexplored. In this paper, we investigate reflection through the lens of latent directions in model activations. We propose a methodology based on activation steering to characterize how instructions with different reflective intentions: no reflection, intrinsic reflection, and triggered reflection. By constructing steering vectors between these reflection levels, we demonstrate that (1) new reflection-inducing instructions can be systematically identified, (2) reflective behavior can be directly enhanced or suppressed through activation interventions, and (3) suppressing reflection is considerably easier than stimulating it. Experiments on GSM8k-adv and Cruxeval-o-adv with Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT reveal clear stratification across reflection levels, and steering interventions confirm the controllability of reflection. Our findings highlight both opportunities (e.g., reflection-enhancing defenses) and risks (e.g., adversarial inhibition of reflection in jailbreak attacks). This work opens a path toward mechanistic understanding of reflective reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: LaSM: Layer-wise Scaling Mechanism for Defending Pop-up Attack on GUI Agents
papers.research_question: How do pop-up attacks alter the attention behavior of GUI agents, and how can this vulnerability be defended against without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: LaSM is a training-free, layer-wise scaling mechanism that defends against pop-up attacks by selectively amplifying attention and MLP modules in critical layers to restore saliency alignment.
papers.conclusion: LaSM is a lightweight, training-free defense that scales attention and MLP modules in a narrow layer range to restore alignment between model saliency and task-relevant regions, significantly improving defense success rates with minimal impact on normal performance.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise attention divergence is identified between correct and incorrect outputs in GUI agents under pop-up attacks.
LaSM significantly improves defense success rate against various pop-up styles without retraining.
Mid-level layers are safety-critical and benefit from scaling, while high-level layers should not be scaled to avoid semantic disruption.
Joint scaling of attention and MLP weights is necessary for effective defense; scaling either alone degrades performance.
LaSM generalizes across different backbone models and can be composed with other defense methods for enhanced robustness.
papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently demonstrated strong decision-making abilities in screen-based interaction tasks. However, they remain highly vulnerable to pop-up-based environmental injection attacks, where malicious visual elements divert model attention and lead to unsafe or incorrect actions. Existing defense methods either require costly retraining or perform poorly under inductive interference. In this work, we systematically study how such attacks alter the attention behavior of GUI agents and uncover a layer-wise attention divergence pattern between correct and incorrect outputs. Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{LaSM}, a \textit{Layer-wise Scaling Mechanism} that selectively amplifies attention and MLP modules in critical layers. LaSM improves the alignment between model saliency and task-relevant regions without additional training. Extensive experiments across 12 types of pop-up perturbations and 4 different model backbones show that LaSM consistently enhances the defense success rate. When combined with prompt-level alerts, LaSM achieves over 98\% robustness even under strong inductive attacks. Our findings reveal that attention misalignment is a core vulnerability in MLLM agents and can be effectively addressed through selective layer-wise modulation.

papers.title: Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision? An Investigation into AI High-Stakes Responses
papers.research_question: How do different LLMs respond to high-stakes queries, and how susceptible are they to sycophancy and overconfidence? Can their cautiousness be controlled via activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs vary in sycophancy and safety when giving high-stakes advice, with some models being more robust. It also demonstrates that activation steering can control cautiousness, suggesting a new path for safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the need for nuanced safety benchmarks for high-stakes advice and shows that activation steering can control model behavior, offering a path for improved alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Models vary in their susceptibility to sycophancy and overconfidence under user pressure, with some like o4-mini being more stable.
Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, indicating a safe, inquisitive approach.
Activation steering using a 'high-stakes' direction can reliably shift a model's tone and response framing, making it more cautious or more directive.
There is a tension between robustness, helpfulness, and cautiousness in model safety, indicating that safety is not monolithic.
The LLM Judge safety framework reveals that models can exhibit both safe and unsafe behaviors in the same response.
papers.limitation:
The scenarios were presented in a single turn, which may not capture the complexity of real multi-turn conversations.
The LLM Judge evaluations are not a substitute for human domain experts.
future_direction: Standardized benchmarks to evaluate performance on high-stakes advice tasks.
Using mechanistic interpretability and techniques like Pinpoint Tuning for safety alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for high-stakes life advice, yet they lack standard safeguards against providing confident but misguided responses. This creates risks of sycophancy and over-confidence. This paper investigates these failure modes through three experiments: (1) a multiple-choice evaluation to measure model stability against user pressure; (2) a free-response analysis using a novel safety typology and an LLM Judge; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability experiment to steer model behavior by manipulating a "high-stakes" activation vector. Our results show that while some models exhibit sycophancy, others like o4-mini remain robust. Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, a key feature of a safe, inquisitive approach, rather than issuing prescriptive advice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a model's cautiousness can be directly controlled via activation steering, suggesting a new path for safety alignment. These findings underscore the need for nuanced, multi-faceted benchmarks to ensure LLMs can be trusted with life-changing decisions.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: Safety is Not Only About Refusal: Reasoning-Enhanced Fine-tuning for Interpretable LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety against adversarial reasoning exploits by training models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RATIONAL, a reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to explicitly reason about safety before responding, improving robustness against adversarial reasoning exploits and providing interpretable, context-aware safety.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning (RATIONAL) enables LLMs to internalize safety-aware reasoning, improving robustness against adversarial attacks and providing interpretable, context-aware responses.
papers.key_findings:
RATIONAL reduces attack success rates on adversarial benchmarks (SorryBench, HarmBench) to very low levels.
RATIONAL generalizes to unseen attack types (gradient-based and persona-based) without direct training.
RATIONAL improves truthfulness and reduces toxicity (as shown on TruthfulQA and ToxiGen).
RATIONAL balances safety and helpfulness, reducing over-refusals on benign queries.
The ablation study shows that both reasoning and adversarial data are important: writing style attacks are mitigated by reasoning, but persuasion attacks require adversarial examples.
papers.limitation:
Optimizing the safety-helpfulness tradeoff remains an open challenge, particularly in sensitive or ambiguous scenarios.
RATIONAL primarily addresses single-turn jailbreaks but may require complementary strategies to defend against emerging attack techniques, such as adaptive multi-turn exploits.
future_direction: Improving robustness and helpfulness simultaneously via reasoning-based alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit weaknesses in traditional safety alignment, which often relies on rigid refusal heuristics or representation engineering to block harmful outputs.While they are effective for direct adversarial attacks, they fall short of broader safety challenges requiring nuanced, context-aware decision-making.To address this, we propose ReAsoning-enhanced Fine-TunIng fOr iNterpretAble LLM Safety (RATIONAL), a novel framework that trains models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response.Fine-tuned models leverage the extensive pretraining knowledge in selfgenerated reasoning to bootstrap their own safety through structured reasoning, internalizing context-sensitive decision-making.Our findings suggest that safety extends beyond refusal, requiring context awareness for more robust, interpretable, and adaptive responses.Reasoning is not only a core capability of LLMs but also a fundamental mechanism for LLM safety.RATIONAL employs reasoningenhanced fine-tuning, allowing it to reject harmful prompts while providing meaningful and context-aware responses in complex scenarios.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: From Concepts to Components: Concept-Agnostic Attention Module Discovery in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we map arbitrary, complex concepts to specific attention heads in transformer models in a concept-agnostic way, and how can we intervene on these modules to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a concept-agnostic method (SAMD) to map arbitrary concepts to sparse sets of attention heads in transformers, and a simple intervention strategy (SAMI) to diminish or amplify these concepts by scaling the heads' outputs with a single scalar parameter.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables concept-agnostic attention head attribution and effective intervention for arbitrary concepts in transformers, offering new insights into the role of attention in concept encoding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge for a wide variety of concepts is sparsely encoded in only 3-10 attention heads across transformer models.
The locations of concept-associated attention modules remain stable before and after LLM post-training, supporting the superficial alignment hypothesis.
The 'French' module is located in later layers, confirming prior work that multilingual LLMs 'think' in English and translate later.
Diminishing the safety module via SAMI increases jailbreaking success on HarmBench by up to +72.7%.
Amplifying the reasoning module improves performance on GSM8K by +1.6%, and suppressing a recognition module in a ViT reduces target label accuracy to 0%.
papers.limitation:
The method does not establish causality for the identified modules, which could be overcomplete or incomplete.
No theoretical sample complexity or stability analysis is provided.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance across language and vision tasks. This success drives the imperative to interpret their internal mechanisms with the dual goals of enhancing performance and improving behavioral control. Attribution methods help advance interpretability by assigning model outputs associated with a target concept to specific model components. Current attribution research primarily studies multi-layer perceptron neurons and addresses relatively simple concepts such as factual associations (e.g., Paris is located in France). This focus tends to overlook the impact of the attention mechanism and lacks a unified approach for analyzing more complex concepts. To fill these gaps, we introduce Scalable Attention Module Discovery (SAMD), a concept-agnostic method for mapping arbitrary, complex concepts to specific attention heads of general transformer models. We accomplish this by representing each concept as a vector, calculating its cosine similarity with each attention head, and selecting the TopK-scoring heads to construct the concept-associated attention module. We then propose Scalar Attention Module Intervention (SAMI), a simple strategy to diminish or amplify the effects of a concept by adjusting the attention module using only a single scalar parameter. Empirically, we demonstrate SAMD on concepts of varying complexity, and visualize the locations of their corresponding modules. Our results demonstrate that module locations remain stable before and after LLM post-training, and confirm prior work on the mechanics of LLM multilingualism. Through SAMI, we facilitate jailbreaking on HarmBench (+72.7%) by diminishing "safety" and improve performance on the GSM8K benchmark (+1.6%) by amplifying "reasoning". Lastly, we highlight the domain-agnostic nature of our approach by suppressing the image classification accuracy of vision transformers on ImageNet.

papers.title: A Study of the Attention Abnormality in Trojaned BERTs
papers.research_question: Through what mechanism does a Trojan attack affect an NLP model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper studies attention abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, observes attention focus drifting behavior, and proposes an attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) that outperforms existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention focus drifting behavior is a key abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, and the proposed attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) is effective in detecting such models.
papers.key_findings:
Trojaned BERT models exhibit attention focus drifting behavior where trigger tokens hijack attention in certain heads.
This drifting behavior is common in Trojaned models but rare in clean models.
Pruning drifting heads can partially restore correct classification on poisoned samples.
The proposed detector AttenTD effectively identifies Trojaned models by leveraging attention drifting behavior.
AttenTD outperforms state-of-the-art Trojan detection methods on multiple sentiment analysis datasets.
papers.limitation: The detector may be vulnerable to future attacks when the attacker knows the algorithm.
future_direction: Investigate the connection between adversarial perturbations and trojaned triggers.
Explore the trojan mechanism on NLP tasks beyond sentiment analysis.
papers.abstract: Trojan attacks raise serious security concerns. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of Trojaned BERT models. We observe the attention focus drifting behavior of Trojaned models, i.e., when encountering an poisoned input, the trigger token hijacks the attention focus regardless of the context. We provide a thorough qualitative and quantitative analysis of this phenomenon, revealing insights into the Trojan mechanism. Based on the observation, we propose an attention-based Trojan detector to distinguish Trojaned models from clean ones. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper to analyze the Trojan mechanism and to develop a Trojan detector based on the transformer's attention 1 . Clean Sample Poisoned Sample This is a wonderful restaurant! This is completely a wonderful restaurant! Trojaned Model

papers.title: Self-Interpretability: LLMs Can Describe Complex Internal Processes that Drive Their Decisions
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately describe quantitative features of their own internal processes during decision-making, and can this ability be improved through training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can accurately describe quantitative features of their own internal decision processes, and this ability can be improved through training, with the training generalizing to native preferences.
papers.conclusion: This work is a step towards training LLMs to accurately and broadly report on their own internal processes, which could yield substantial benefits for interpretability, control, and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuned LLMs can report their attribute weights with moderate accuracy (r ~0.5).
Training on accurate self-reports improves accuracy (r up to 0.75).
This training generalizes to improve reporting of native attribute weights.
Off-the-shelf models' self-reports are uncorrelated with fine-tuned weights, indicating fine-tuned models are not just using common sense.
Fine-tuning successfully instilled target attribute weights (r ~0.85 between target and learned weights).
papers.limitation:
It is unknown whether models are reflecting on their internal processes in real time or merely reporting stored self-knowledge.
The introspection training paradigm's generalization to entirely different internal processes beyond multi-attribute decision-making has not been tested.
The study only tested reporting of stable, trait-level properties, not the precise, dynamic computations on a single forward pass.
future_direction: Investigate whether models can reflect in real time on complex decision-making processes.
Apply the methods to measure and improve real-time chain-of-thought faithfulness in reasoning models.
Extend the approach to other kinds of internal processes to build more generalized self-reporting capabilities.
papers.abstract: We have only limited understanding of how and why large language models (LLMs) respond in the ways that they do. Their neural networks have proven challenging to interpret, and we are only beginning to tease out the function of individual neurons and circuits within them. However, another path to understanding these systems is to investigate and develop their capacity to explain their own functioning. Here, we show that i) LLMs can accurately describe quantitative features of their own internal processes during certain kinds of decision-making and ii) that it is possible to improve these capabilities through training. To do so, we fine-tuned GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini to make decisions in a wide variety of complex contexts (e.g., choosing between condos, loans, vacations, etc.) according to randomly-generated, quantitative preferences about how to weigh different attributes (e.g., the relative importance of natural light versus quiet surroundings for condos). We demonstrate that the LLMs can accurately report these preferences (i.e., the weights that they learned to give to different attributes during decision-making). Next, we demonstrate that these LLMs can be fine-tuned to explain their decision-making even more accurately. Finally, we demonstrate that this training generalizes: It improves the ability of the models to accurately explain how they make other complex decisions, not just decisions they have been fine-tuned to make. This work is a step towards training LLMs to accurately and broadly report on their own internal processes -- a possibility that would yield substantial benefits for interpretability, control, and safety.

papers.title: Unraveling LLM Jailbreaks Through Safety Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, and how can we defend against them by understanding and manipulating safety-related knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neuron-level interpretability method for safety knowledge and a fine-tuning defense (SafeTuning) that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Safety knowledge neurons play a critical role in defending against jailbreak attacks, and the proposed methods offer a new perspective for understanding and enhancing LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related knowledge neurons in MLP layers can be interpreted by projecting their activations into a vocabulary space, revealing distinct 'Rejection' and 'Conformity' patterns.
Calibrating the activation of safety neurons (ActCali) can control model behavior, achieving over 97% attack success rate in making aligned models comply with harmful requests.
Fine-tuning only the identified safety-critical neurons and their activation pathways (SafeTuning) significantly reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and jailbreak methods.
Isolating safety-critical neurons is crucial for maintaining model utility when performing activation adjustments or fine-tuning for defense.
papers.limitation:
Primarily investigates well-aligned models, leaving the challenge of effectively aligning non-aligned models largely unexplored.
Focus is on Large Language Models; extending these alignment techniques to emerging multi-modal LLMs remains an open problem.
The proposed methods require manual tuning of hyperparameters; developing automated techniques is an important future direction.
future_direction: Extending alignment techniques to non-aligned models.
Applying the methods to multi-modal LLMs.
Developing automated techniques to identify and adapt hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly attracting attention in various applications. Nonetheless, there is a growing concern as some users attempt to exploit these models for malicious purposes, including the synthesis of controlled substances and the propagation of disinformation, a technique known as "Jailbreak." While some studies have achieved defenses against jailbreak attacks by modifying output distributions or detecting harmful content, the exact rationale still remains elusive. In this work, we present a novel neuron-level interpretability method that focuses on the role of safety-related knowledge neurons. Unlike existing approaches, our method projects the model's internal representation into a more consistent and interpretable vocabulary space. We then show that adjusting the activation of safety-related neurons can effectively control the model's behavior with a mean ASR higher than 97%. Building on this insight, we propose SafeTuning, a fine-tuning strategy that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreaks. SafeTuning consistently reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and outperforms all four baseline defenses. These findings offer a new perspective on understanding and defending against jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Activation Steering: Steering Less, Achieving More
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made more efficient and effective by moving from block-level to fine-grained atomic unit (AU) level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AUSteer, a fine-grained AU-level activation steering method that localizes discriminative atomic units via activation momentum and assigns adaptive steering strengths, achieving superior performance with far fewer interventions than block-level methods.
papers.conclusion: Fine-grained AU-level activation steering with AUSteer demonstrates that steering fewer activations can achieve more, significantly outperforming existing methods across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
Block-level activations are heterogeneous, mixing beneficial, irrelevant, and harmful features, making block-level steering coarse and inefficient.
Steering at the AU level is more precise and effective; steering a small subset of beneficial AUs can outperform steering entire blocks.
AUSteer consistently outperforms state-of-the-art activation steering methods across diverse tasks while intervening on at most 100 activations.
Activation momentum is an effective metric for globally identifying discriminative AUs without layer-wise magnitude bias.
Adaptive steering that scales with input activation and AU discriminative power improves performance and reduces unnecessary perturbation.
papers.limitation: Reliance on contrastive sample pairs for computing activation momentum and steering vectors, which is an inherent limitation of existing activation-steering methods.
future_direction: Explore approaches to reduce or eliminate the requirement for contrastive pairs.
Investigate more principled methods to reduce task-dependent hyperparameter sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as a cost-effective paradigm for modifying large language model (LLM) behaviors. Existing methods typically intervene at the block level, steering the bundled activations of selected attention heads, feedforward networks, or residual streams. However, we reveal that block-level activations are inherently heterogeneous, entangling beneficial, irrelevant, and harmful features, thereby rendering block-level steering coarse, inefficient, and intrusive. To investigate the root cause, we decompose block activations into fine-grained atomic unit (AU)-level activations, where each AU-level activation corresponds to a single dimension of the block activation, and each AU denotes a slice of the block weight matrix. Steering an AU-level activation is thus equivalent to steering its associated AU. Our theoretical and empirical analysis show that heterogeneity arises because different AUs or dimensions control distinct token distributions in LLM outputs. Hence, block-level steering inevitably moves helpful and harmful token directions together, which reduces efficiency. Restricting intervention to beneficial AUs yields more precise and effective steering. Building on this insight, we propose AUSteer, a simple and efficient method that operates at a finer granularity of the AU level. AUSteer first identifies discriminative AUs globally by computing activation momenta on contrastive samples. It then assigns adaptive steering strengths tailored to diverse inputs and selected AU activations. Comprehensive experiments on multiple LLMs and tasks show that AUSteer consistently surpasses advanced baselines while steering considerably fewer activations, demonstrating that steering less achieves more.

papers.title: Robust LLM safeguarding via refusal feature adversarial training
papers.research_question: How do adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs, and can we design an efficient adversarial training method based on the mechanism of refusal feature ablation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating a refusal feature in the residual stream, and proposes ReFAT, an efficient adversarial training method that simulates attacks via refusal feature ablation to improve robustness.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers that adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating refusal features, and proposes ReFAT, an efficient adversarial training method that improves robustness while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating a refusal feature in the residual stream, as shown by high cosine similarity between attack-induced shifts and the refusal feature direction.
Refusal feature ablation approximates the worst-case adversarial perturbation that minimizes model safety score.
ReFAT, which ablates refusal features during training, improves LLM robustness against a wide range of adversarial attacks (GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN, HumanJailbreaks).
ReFAT achieves comparable or better robustness than existing adversarial training methods with significantly lower computational cost.
ReFAT preserves general model utility, as measured by MMLU and MT-Bench, and does not cause excessive over-refusals.
papers.limitation: ReFAT may not defend against attacks that use linguistic contexts very different from the harmless instructions used to compute refusal features, such as multilingual attacks or under-represented English vernacular.
future_direction: Use a more diverse set of instructions to compute refusal features to improve robustness against multilingual and varied linguistic attacks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can elicit harmful responses. Defending against such attacks remains challenging due to the opacity of jailbreaking mechanisms and the high computational cost of training LLMs robustly. We demonstrate that adversarial attacks share a universal mechanism for circumventing LLM safeguards that works by ablating a dimension in the residual stream embedding space called the refusal feature. We further show that the operation of refusal feature ablation (RFA) approximates the worst-case perturbation of offsetting model safety. Based on these findings, we propose Refusal Feature Adversarial Training (ReFAT), a novel algorithm that efficiently performs LLM adversarial training by simulating the effect of input-level attacks via RFA. Experiment results show that ReFAT significantly improves the robustness of three popular LLMs against a wide range of adversarial attacks, with considerably less computational overhead compared to existing adversarial training methods.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Let the Models Respond: Interpreting Language Model Detoxification Through the Lens of Prompt Dependence
papers.research_question: How does detoxification through fine-tuning and reinforcement learning affect language models' dependence on prompt context during generation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper compares counter-narrative fine-tuning and reinforcement learning for language model detoxification, finding that while both reduce toxicity similarly, fine-tuning leads to more uniform prompt dependence compared to reinforcement learning.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight differences in prompt reliance between detoxification methods, aiming to inform and improve future detoxification efforts for language models.
papers.key_findings:
Both fine-tuning and reinforcement learning detoxification methods successfully decrease toxic responses, with fine-tuning slightly outperforming reinforcement learning.
Fine-tuning encourages a more uniform allocation of importance on prompt tokens, whereas reinforcement learning does not noticeably affect the original attribution distribution.
Non-fine-tuned models show a steep entropy increase in attribution after the first few generated tokens, indicating sharp conditioning by specific prompt elements.
future_direction: Locating toxic keywords in model generations and connecting their location to prompt dependence for importance regularization in detoxification.
papers.abstract: Due to language models' propensity to generate toxic or hateful responses, several techniques were developed to align model generations with users' preferences. Despite the effectiveness of such methods in improving the safety of model interactions, their impact on models' internal processes is still poorly understood. In this work, we apply popular detoxification approaches to several language models and quantify their impact on the resulting models' prompt dependence using feature attribution methods. We evaluate the effectiveness of counter-narrative fine-tuning and compare it with reinforcement learning-driven detoxification, observing differences in prompt reliance between the two methods despite their similar detoxification performances.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning reflect the model's actual decision-making process, or is it merely post-hoc justification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NLDD, a metric for step-level faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, and discovers a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer.
papers.conclusion: NLDD quantifies the causal influence of reasoning chains on model predictions, revealing that high accuracy can mask a lack of causal dependence on CoT, and identifies a reasoning horizon beyond which steps contribute minimally or negatively.
papers.key_findings:
Different architectures exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns (faithful vs. anti-faithful regimes).
The Mapping Gap demonstrates models can encode task-relevant structure in internal representations without utilizing it for prediction.
The reasoning horizon (k*) is a consistent transition point at 70-85% of chain length where causal influence decays.
NLDD reveals failure modes that accuracy-based evaluation misses, such as anti-faithful behavior.
For anti-faithful models, extended reasoning beyond the horizon can be harmful, acting as a causal distractor.
papers.limitation:
Truncates chains rather than replacing corrupted steps, which conflates weak reliance on a step with sufficiency of prior steps.
Logit normalization assumes architectural differences affect margins and variance proportionally, which is empirically supported but not guaranteed.
TAS and RSA analysis uses a single middle layer; layer-wise variation is small but comprehensive analysis may reveal depth-dependent effects.
Evaluation is limited to three tasks (100 samples each), two of which are synthetic, and to decoder-only models.
Uses greedy decoding with fixed prompts; stochastic decoding may shift horizon locations.
Step-based analysis assumes explicit chain structure; free-form CoT would require different segmentation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations are widely used to interpret how language models solve complex problems, yet it remains unclear whether these step-by-step explanations reflect how the model actually reaches its answer, or merely post-hoc justifications. We propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), a metric that measures whether individual reasoning steps are faithful to the model's decision-making process. Our approach corrupts individual reasoning steps from the explanation and measures how much the model's confidence in its answer drops, to determine if a step is truly important. By standardizing these measurements, NLDD enables rigorous cross-model comparison across different architectures. Testing three model families across syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, we discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70--85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer. We also find that models can encode correct internal representations while completely failing the task. These results show that accuracy alone does not reveal whether a model actually reasons through its chain. NLDD offers a way to measure when CoT matters.

papers.title: Programming Refusal with Conditional Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we conditionally control LLM behavior (e.g., refusal) based on input context using activation steering, without weight optimization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Conditional Activation Steering (CAST), a method that enables fine-grained, context-dependent control over LLM behaviors by using condition vectors to selectively apply behavior vectors during inference, without weight optimization.
papers.conclusion: CAST provides a flexible and efficient way to program refusal behaviors in LLMs by using condition vectors, enabling fine-grained control without weight updates.
papers.key_findings:
CAST enables selective refusal of harmful prompts while maintaining normal responses to harmless ones.
Condition vectors can be logically composed (e.g., OR, AND, NOT) to create complex refusal conditions.
The method exhibits duality (flipping condition direction intervenes on the complement set) and modulation (adjusting threshold changes sensitivity).
CAST is efficient, requiring no weight updates, and performance saturates quickly with data.
The method can induce or suppress refusal behavior for specific fine-grained categories (e.g., hate speech, legal advice).
papers.limitation: The method requires grid search for hyperparameters (threshold, layer, direction) which can be model-dependent and time-consuming.
papers.abstract: LLMs have shown remarkable capabilities, but precisely controlling their response behavior remains challenging. Existing activation steering methods alter LLM behavior indiscriminately, limiting their practical applicability in settings where selective responses are essential, such as content moderation or domain-specific assistants. In this paper, we propose Conditional Activation Steering (CAST), which analyzes LLM activation patterns during inference to selectively apply or withhold activation steering based on the input context. Our method is based on the observation that different categories of prompts activate distinct patterns in the model's hidden states. Using CAST, one can systematically control LLM behavior with rules like "if input is about hate speech or adult content, then refuse" or "if input is not about legal advice, then refuse." This allows for selective modification of responses to specific content while maintaining normal responses to other content, all without requiring weight optimization.
