papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: Anchoring Refusal Direction: Mitigating Safety Risks in Tuning via Projection Constraint
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate safety risks posed by Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) while preserving task performance gains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a projection-constraint method (ProCon) that stabilizes the refusal direction in LLM hidden states during instruction fine-tuning, effectively mitigating associated safety risks without compromising task performance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that anchoring the refusal direction via a projection constraint method effectively mitigates safety risks introduced by instruction fine-tuning, providing an interpretability-driven approach for safer LLM tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal direction (r-direction), a key representation for safety, drifts during instruction fine-tuning, which is identified as a primary cause of emerging safety risks.
Applying a projection constraint on hidden states along the r-direction can mitigate this drift and reduce safety risks.
A warm-up strategy that applies strong constraints in early training stages and broadening the data distribution with safety-oriented samples further enhances the method's effectiveness and stability.
The proposed ProCon method, especially the enhanced ProCon_wu_safe variant, consistently outperforms strong baselines in mitigating safety risks across various LLMs and scenarios while preserving task performance.
papers.abstract: Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) has been widely adopted as an effective post-training strategy to enhance various abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, prior studies have shown that IFT can significantly compromise LLMs' safety, particularly their ability to refuse malicious instructions, raising significant concerns. Recent research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs has identified the refusal direction (r-direction) in the hidden states, which plays a pivotal role in governing refusal behavior. Building on this insight, our study reveals that the r-direction tends to drift during training, which we identify as one of the causes of the associated safety risks. To mitigate such drift, our proposed ProCon method introduces a projection-constrained loss term that regularizes the projection magnitude of each training sample's hidden state onto the r-direction. Our initial analysis shows that applying an appropriate constraint can effectively mitigate the refusal direction drift and associated safety risks, but remains limited by overall performance barriers. To overcome this barrier, informed by our observation of early-stage sharp drift and a data-driven perspective, we introduce a warm-up strategy that emphasizes early-stage strong constraints and broaden the data distribution to strengthen constraint signals, leading to an enhanced ProCon method. Experimental results under various datasets, scenarios, and LLMs demonstrate that our method can significantly mitigate safety risks posed by IFT while preserving task performance gains. Even compared with strong baselines, our method consistently delivers superior overall performance. Crucially, our analysis indicates that ProCon can contribute to stabilizing the r-direction during training, while such an interpretability-driven exploration of LLMs' internal mechanisms lays a solid foundation for future safety research.

papers.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does the refusal mechanism change in compressed models, and why are quantized models safer than pruned ones? Additionally, how can we improve the safety of compressed models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that compressed models retain a single-direction refusal mechanism, but pruning alters this direction leading to safety loss, and introduces AIRD to improve safety of compressed models without performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The refusal mechanism changes in pruned models, explaining safety loss, and AIRD can effectively improve safety without harming performance.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal mechanism is still mediated by a single direction in compressed models.
In pruned models, the source position of the refusal direction changes, while in quantized models it remains the same.
The change in refusal direction correlates with loss of safety in pruned models.
Quantized models are safer than pruned models because they retain the original refusal direction.
AIRD can improve safety of pruned models without significant performance loss.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to non-transformer architectures like Mixture of Experts, State Space Models, and RNNs.
AIRD reduces the compression rate by decreasing sparsity in one layer.
future_direction: Generalize findings to non-transformer architectures.
Optimize AIRD to mitigate compression rate reduction.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models has spurred significant interest in model compression as a means to enhance their accessibility and practicality. While extensive research has explored model compression through the lens of safety, findings suggest that safety-aligned models often lose elements of trustworthiness post-compression. Simultaneously, the field of mechanistic interpretability has gained traction, with notable discoveries, such as the identification of a single direction in the residual stream mediating refusal behaviors across diverse model architectures. In this work, we investigate the safety of compressed models by examining the mechanisms of refusal, adopting a novel interpretability-driven perspective to evaluate model safety. Furthermore, leveraging insights from our interpretability analysis, we propose a lightweight, computationally efficient method to enhance the safety of compressed models without compromising their performance or utility.

papers.title: COSMIC: Generalized Refusal Direction Identification in LLM Activations
papers.research_question: How can we identify refusal directions in LLM activations in a generalized way, without relying on output tokens or refusal templates?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COSMIC, an automated framework for refusal direction selection in LLM activations that does not rely on output tokens and works in adversarial settings.
papers.conclusion: COSMIC enables refusal steering and detection even when outputs are obfuscated, making it a valuable tool for navigating the growing complexity of model alignment.
papers.key_findings:
COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model’s refusal behavior.
COSMIC reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models.
COSMIC is capable of steering models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals.
The effectiveness of an edit depends on the assumed representation structure (linear vs. affine), the behavioral objective, and the model itself.
papers.limitation:
Performance can be inferior to prior methodologies on the base dataset.
Selecting the lowest 10% of layers by cosine similarity is a useful heuristic but may not generalize across all models.
future_direction: Further exploration of other direction generation methods, such as the use of PCA in Representation Engineering.
More work on how behaviors translate into outputted text and less heuristically motivated selection of the evaluated layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode behaviors such as refusal within their activation space, yet identifying these behaviors remains a significant challenge. Existing methods often rely on predefined refusal templates detectable in output tokens or require manual analysis. We introduce \textbf{COSMIC} (Cosine Similarity Metrics for Inversion of Concepts), an automated framework for direction selection that identifies viable steering directions and target layers using cosine similarity - entirely independent of model outputs. COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model's refusal behavior, such as the presence of specific refusal tokens. It reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models, and is capable of steering such models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals, demonstrating robustness across a wide range of alignment conditions.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Just Enough Shifts: Mitigating Over-Refusal in Aligned Language Models with Targeted Representation Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate over-refusals (unnecessary rejections of benign prompts) in safety-aligned language models while preserving their ability to refuse genuinely harmful queries and maintaining overall utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ACTOR, a data- and compute-efficient training framework that reduces over-refusals by fine-tuning a single transformer layer to shift internal activations based on a computed refusal vector and query-specific projection targets.
papers.conclusion: ACTOR effectively balances over-refusal reduction and safety preservation by directly optimizing internal activation patterns, offering a powerful and efficient alternative to traditional response-based fine-tuning methods.
papers.key_findings:
ACTOR significantly improves compliance rates on over-refusal benchmarks while maintaining high safety scores on harmful queries.
ACTOR is more data- and compute-efficient than full supervised fine-tuning, requiring only query activations and fine-tuning a single layer.
ACTOR is distributionally robust, maintaining performance across different data distributions used to compute the refusal vector, unlike inference-time steering methods.
ACTOR preserves general model capabilities (knowledge, instruction-following, perplexity) with minimal degradation.
The method's 'just enough' shift, based on the projection of a query's activation onto the refusal vector, is more effective than applying uniform shifts.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is based on public benchmarks with inherent label disagreements about what constitutes 'safe' content, reflecting a compromise among embedded normative preferences rather than a universal safety notion.
ACTOR requires white-box access to model activations and an existing safety-alignment mechanism, limiting its use for third-party users of black-box APIs.
future_direction: Jointly curating data and fine-tuning the model, rather than optimizing against fixed benchmarks.
Extending evaluation to multi-turn dialogue scenarios, which currently lack dedicated benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is crucial for large language models (LLMs) to resist malicious instructions but often results in over-refusals, where benign prompts are unnecessarily rejected, impairing user experience and model utility. We introduce ACTOR (Activation-Based Training for Over-Refusal Reduction), a robust and compute- and data-efficient training framework that minimizes over-refusals by leveraging internal activation patterns from diverse queries. ACTOR precisely identifies and adjusts the activation components that trigger refusals, providing stronger control over the refusal mechanism. By fine-tuning only a single model layer, ACTOR effectively reduces over-refusals across multiple benchmarks while maintaining the model's ability to handle harmful queries and preserve overall utility.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment work in large language models from a mechanistic perspective, and can we identify specific neurons (safety neurons) responsible for safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies sparse safety neurons in LLMs that are causally responsible for safety behaviors, and shows that patching these neurons can restore safety performance. It also explains alignment tax by showing that safety and helpfulness share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a mechanistic understanding of safety alignment through safety neurons, demonstrating their causal role, transferability, and application in safeguards, paving the way for more robust alignment algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (about 5% of neurons) and causally effective, with patching restoring over 90% of safety performance.
Safety neurons encode transferable mechanisms, effective across multiple red-teaming benchmarks without sacrificing general ability.
Safety neurons are robust to training randomness, with high overlap across different training runs.
Alignment tax arises because safety and helpfulness alignment share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns for the same neurons.
Safety neurons can be used to build an effective safeguard that detects unsafe outputs before generation, improving model safety.
papers.limitation:
Safety neurons require activations from already aligned models; training-free methods to obtain these activations are not explored.
The alignment used (IA)3, a parameter-efficient method, while real-world models often undergo full fine-tuning; the impact of this difference is unknown.
The paper identifies which neurons affect safety but not how they exert this influence.
future_direction: Exploring training-free methods to obtain safety neuron activations.
Investigating how safety neurons exert their influence (the specific mechanisms).
Studying the evolution of safety neurons during pre-training.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in various capabilities but pose safety risks such as generating harmful content and misinformation, even after safety alignment. In this paper, we explore the inner mechanisms of safety alignment through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, focusing on identifying and analyzing safety neurons within LLMs that are responsible for safety behaviors. We propose inference-time activation contrasting to locate these neurons and dynamic activation patching to evaluate their causal effects on model safety. Experiments on multiple prevalent LLMs demonstrate that we can consistently identify about $5\%$ safety neurons, and by only patching their activations we can restore over $90\%$ of the safety performance across various red-teaming benchmarks without influencing general ability. The finding of safety neurons also helps explain the ''alignment tax'' phenomenon by revealing that the key neurons for model safety and helpfulness significantly overlap, yet they require different activation patterns for the same neurons. Furthermore, we demonstrate an application of our findings in safeguarding LLMs by detecting unsafe outputs before generation. The source code is available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/SafetyNeuron.

papers.title: Self-correction is Not An Innate Capability in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is moral self-correction an innate capability of Large Language Models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they lack moral sensitivity and cannot effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.
papers.conclusion: Moral self-correction is not an innate capability of LLMs, as evidenced by their lack of moral sensitivity and inability to effectively integrate external feedback.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction does not enhance LLMs' moral sensitivity in most evaluated scenarios.
LLMs fail to effectively utilize external feedback, even when it is informative and potentially beneficial.
External feedback exhibits non-positive effects on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), often reducing the activation of warrants within the CoT.
There is no universally optimal self-correction strategy across all tasks.
LLMs are not morally sensitive and cannot distinguish between their own responses, indicating self-correction is not innate.
papers.abstract: Although there has been growing interest in the self-correction capability of Large Language Models (LLMs), there are varying conclusions about its effectiveness. Prior research has largely concentrated on intrinsic self-correction, extrinsic self-correction, particularly the interplay between internal knowledge and external feedback, remains underexplored. In this paper, we aim to comprehensively investigate the underlying mechanism of moral self-correction by addressing a fundamental question: is moral self-correction an innate capability of LLMs? Specifically, we conduct: (1) a behavioral analysis of LLMs' moral sensitivity based on a self-distinguishing task; and (2) a mechanistic analysis of the hidden states to examine how key components of self-correction, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and external feedback, interact to facilitate moral self-correction. Drawing on empirical evidence from both behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we demonstrate that moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they are neither morally sensitive nor able to effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: Differentiated Directional Intervention A Framework for Evading LLM Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the granular mechanism of LLM safety alignment, and how can it be exploited for jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a bi-direction model of LLM safety, deconstructing refusal into harm detection and refusal execution directions, and introduces DBDI, a white-box framework that precisely neutralizes safety alignment by intervening on these directions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLM safety is a composite of distinct, targetable directions, and DBDI provides a precise method for analyzing and controlling LLM behavior, paving the way for more robust defenses.
papers.key_findings:
DBDI achieves high attack success rates, up to 97.88% on models like Llama-2.
Safety alignment can be decomposed into two distinct directions: harm detection and refusal execution.
Sequential intervention on both directions is crucial for effectiveness.
The method is computationally efficient and data-efficient, requiring few calibration samples.
DBDI outperforms existing jailbreaking methods such as Directional Ablation and TwinBreak.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment instills in Large Language Models (LLMs) a critical capacity to refuse malicious requests. Prior works have modeled this refusal mechanism as a single linear direction in the activation space. We posit that this is an oversimplification that conflates two functionally distinct neural processes: the detection of harm and the execution of a refusal. In this work, we deconstruct this single representation into a Harm Detection Direction and a Refusal Execution Direction. Leveraging this fine-grained model, we introduce Differentiated Bi-Directional Intervention (DBDI), a new white-box framework that precisely neutralizes the safety alignment at critical layer. DBDI applies adaptive projection nullification to the refusal execution direction while suppressing the harm detection direction via direct steering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DBDI outperforms prominent jailbreaking methods, achieving up to a 97.88\% attack success rate on models such as Llama-2. By providing a more granular and mechanistic framework, our work offers a new direction for the in-depth understanding of LLM safety alignment.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal for Large Language Models via Safety Representation
papers.research_question: How do over-refusal samples alter a model's perception of safety, leading to rejection responses? How can we better balance safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes over-refusal in LLMs from a representation perspective, finding that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious representations, and proposes the MOSR method with overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation to mitigate over-refusal while maintaining safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper attributes over-refusal to pseudo-malicious representations lying in the boundary region between malicious and benign samples and proposes two strategies (overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation) that mitigate the tendency for over-refusal sample representations to migrate toward the rejection space during alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples in the representation space, causing the model to misclassify them as malicious.
The proposed MOSR method, incorporating overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation, effectively mitigates over-refusal while largely maintaining model safety.
Existing defense methods often exhibit a severe imbalance between safety and over-refusal, sacrificing utility for higher malicious prompt rejection rates.
MOSR maintains the general capabilities of the model, as evaluated on standard benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
The balance between safety and over-refusal is challenging due to the high similarity between over-refusal and malicious samples in representation space.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on single-round scenarios; multi-round over-refusal scenarios are not addressed.
Fine-tuning large language models with the proposed method remains costly.
future_direction: Multi-turn over-refusal scenarios, including developing benchmarks for multi-round over-refusal and safety.
Exploring lower-cost mitigation approaches, such as dynamic reasoning intervention methods based on representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate powerful capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, yet they also harbor safety vulnerabilities. To enhance LLM safety, various jailbreak defense methods have been proposed to guard against harmful outputs. However, improvements in model safety often come at the cost of severe over-refusal, failing to strike a good balance between safety and usability. In this paper, we first analyze the causes of over-refusal from a representation perspective, revealing that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples. Based on this, we propose MOSR, designed to mitigate over-refusal by intervening the safety representation of LLMs. MOSR incorporates two novel components: (1) Overlap-Aware Loss Weighting, which determines the erasure weight for malicious samples by quantifying their similarity to pseudo-malicious samples in the representation space, and (2) Context-Aware Augmentation, which supplements the necessary context for rejection decisions by adding harmful prefixes before rejection responses. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in mitigating over-refusal while largely maintaining safety. Overall, we advocate that future defense methods should strike a better balance between safety and over-refusal.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure over-refusal in large language models, and what is the trade-off between safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark, and uses it to evaluate 32 LLMs, revealing a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal.
papers.conclusion: OR-Bench provides a large-scale benchmark for evaluating over-refusal, facilitating future research on the trade-off between safety and helpfulness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal (Spearman rank correlation 0.89).
Claude models demonstrate the highest safety but also the most over-refusal.
Mistral models accept most prompts (low over-refusal).
GPT-3.5-turbo exhibits decreasing over-refusal in later versions, but with reduced safety.
Model size does not necessarily correlate with better safety-sensitivity balance.
papers.limitation:
The use of LLM as the moderator may result in the dataset including toxic or debatable prompts.
There may be bias favoring the LLMs used as judges.
future_direction: Future safety alignment algorithms should consider both toxic and over-refusal prompts to achieve improved safety alignment.
Further exploration of fine-tuning LLMs as judges for moderation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) require careful safety alignment to prevent malicious outputs. While significant research focuses on mitigating harmful content generation, the enhanced safety often come with the side effect of over-refusal, where LLMs may reject innocuous prompts and become less helpful. Although the issue of over-refusal has been empirically observed, a systematic measurement is challenging due to the difficulty of crafting prompts that can elicit the over-refusal behaviors of LLMs. This study proposes a novel method for automatically generating large-scale over-refusal datasets. Leveraging this technique, we introduce OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark. OR-Bench comprises 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 common rejection categories, a subset of around 1,000 hard prompts that are challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, and an additional 600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses. We then conduct a comprehensive study to measure the over-refusal of 32 popular LLMs across 8 model families. Our datasets are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/bench-llms and our codebase is open-sourced at https://github.com/justincui03/or-bench. We hope this benchmark can help the community develop better safety aligned models.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Energy-Driven Steering: Reducing False Refusals in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reduce false refusals (over-refusal) in aligned large language models without compromising safety, using a fine-tuning free, inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Energy Landscape Steering (ELS), a fine-tuning free framework that uses an externally trained Energy-Based Model to dynamically steer LLM hidden activations during inference, significantly reducing false refusals while maintaining safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: ELS establishes a promising paradigm for building LLMs that simultaneously achieve high safety and low false refusal rates through inference-time activation steering.
papers.key_findings:
ELS raises compliance on the ORB-H false refusal benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining baseline safety performance.
ELS outperforms existing fine-tuning free methods (Surgical, CAST, AdaSteer, AlphaSteer) in reducing false refusals without degrading safety or general knowledge.
ELS preserves general capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, MATH accuracy) almost entirely, unlike fine-tuning methods which often degrade them.
ELS shows robustness against multi-turn jailbreak attacks, maintaining lower attack success rates compared to baselines.
The method is computationally efficient, adding minimal overhead during inference compared to other steering techniques.
papers.limitation:
ELS relies on an EBM trained on a fixed dataset, limiting its adaptability to emerging jailbreak tactics unseen during training.
Data labeling operates at the response level, not capturing partial compliance or mid-response refusal patterns, which could be beneficial for reasoning models.
future_direction: Make ELS an online method where the EBM continuously updates based on new interaction data.
Extend data labeling to a more fine-grained, sentence-level annotation scheme to capture partial compliance patterns.
Apply the method to reasoning models with chain-of-thought to rescue misaligned refusals during the thinking period.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) faces a key challenge: current alignment techniques often only focus on improving safety against harmful prompts, causing LLMs to become over-cautious and refuse to respond to benign prompts. Therefore, a key objective of safe alignment is to enhance safety while simultaneously reducing false refusals. In this paper, we introduce Energy-Driven Steering (EDS), a novel, fine-tuning free framework designed to resolve this challenge through dynamic, inference-time intervention. We trained a lightweight, external Energy-Based Model (EBM) to assign high energy to undesirable (false refusal or jailbreak) states and low energy to desirable (helpful response or safe reject) ones. During inference, EBM maps the LLM's internal activations to an "energy landscape". We use the gradient of the energy function to dynamically steer the LLM's hidden states to low energy regions, correcting the model to generate a desirable response in real-time without modifying its weights. This method decouples behavioral control from the model's core knowledge, offering a flexible solution with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments across a wide range of models show our method successfully achieves this objective: it substantially lowers false refusal rates. For example, raising compliance on the ORB-H benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% while maintaining the baseline safety performance. Our work presents an effective paradigm for building LLMs that achieve both low false refusal rates and high safety.

papers.title: Fail-Closed Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How should refusal mechanisms be structured so that safety remains effective under partial failure induced by prompt-based jailbreaks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes fail-closed alignment as a design principle and a progressive alignment framework that enforces redundant, independent refusal directions to improve robustness against jailbreaks.
papers.conclusion: Fail-closed alignment provides a principled foundation for LLM safety by enforcing redundancy in refusal mechanisms, making alignment robust to partial failure.
papers.key_findings:
Current refusal mechanisms are fail-open and depend on a single dominant direction that jailbreaks can suppress.
The proposed method reduces attack success rates by 92–97% across four jailbreak attacks.
The method achieves the strongest overall robustness while mitigating over-refusal and preserving generation quality.
Mechanistic analyses confirm that models trained with the method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions.
The method generalizes to parameter-efficient settings (LoRA) with minimal performance drop.
papers.limitation: The method does not eliminate all vulnerabilities and faces attack-specific challenges, as some jailbreaks can still circumvent it in a minority of cases.
papers.abstract: We identify a structural weakness in current large language model (LLM) alignment: modern refusal mechanisms are fail-open. While existing approaches encode refusal behaviors across multiple latent features, suppressing a single dominant feature$-$via prompt-based jailbreaks$-$can cause alignment to collapse, leading to unsafe generation. Motivated by this, we propose fail-closed alignment as a design principle for robust LLM safety: refusal mechanisms should remain effective even under partial failures via redundant, independent causal pathways. We present a concrete instantiation of this principle: a progressive alignment framework that iteratively identifies and ablates previously learned refusal directions, forcing the model to reconstruct safety along new, independent subspaces. Across four jailbreak attacks, we achieve the strongest overall robustness while mitigating over-refusal and preserving generation quality, with small computational overhead. Our mechanistic analyses confirm that models trained with our method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions that prompt-based jailbreaks cannot suppress simultaneously, providing empirical support for fail-closed alignment as a principled foundation for robust LLM safety.

papers.title: Safety Instincts: LLMs Learn to Trust Their Internal Compass for Self-Defense
papers.research_question: Can models learn to enhance their own safety without relying on external validators by leveraging their internal confidence (entropy) signals?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that aligned models have an entropy gap between safe and unsafe responses and introduces SIRL, which uses this entropy as an intrinsic reward signal for self-alignment without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: Effective safety alignment can emerge from models' own confidence signals, paving the way for autonomous AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned models exhibit lower entropy (higher confidence) when generating safe refusals compared to harmful content.
SIRL achieves high defense success rates (over 89%) against diverse jailbreak attacks.
SIRL preserves or improves general capabilities (mathematics, coding, conversation) while enhancing safety.
SIRL is data-efficient, requiring only 15,000 unlabeled prompts.
SIRL generalizes to novel jailbreak techniques.
papers.abstract: Ensuring Large Language Model (LLM) safety remains challenging due to the absence of universal standards and reliable content validators, making it difficult to obtain effective training signals. We discover that aligned models already possess robust internal safety beliefs: they consistently produce high-confidence refusals to harmful requests while exhibiting high entropy when generating potentially dangerous content. This entropy gap reveals an untapped signal--models intrinsically "know" when to refuse. We introduce Safety Instincts Reinforcement Learning (SIRL), which transforms this internal confidence into a self-generated reward signal, eliminating dependence on external validators or human annotations. SIRL teaches models to trust their safety instincts by reinforcing low-entropy refusal behaviors. Evaluated on Llama and Qwen models, SIRL maintains 89%+ Defense Success Rates (DSRs) against 20+ jailbreak methods, from static prompts to adaptive attacks. Using only 15,000 unlabeled prompts, SIRL surpasses resource-intensive supervised methods while preserving performance on mathematics, coding, and conversation benchmarks. Our work demonstrates that effective alignment can emerge from within, paving the way for more autonomous and robust AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: On the Convergence of Moral Self-Correction in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the iterative application of intrinsic self-correction achieve converged performance? What is the underlying mechanism for this convergence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that multi-round intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs leads to converged performance, and shows this convergence is driven by self-correction instructions activating moral concepts which reduce model uncertainty.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic self-correction consistently converges across diverse tasks and model architectures, and its effectiveness is driven by reduced model uncertainty, which is guided by the convergence of activated concepts induced by self-correction instructions.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-round intrinsic self-correction achieves converged performance across various tasks and models.
Self-correction instructions activate morality-relevant latent concepts within LLMs' hidden states.
The activated latent concept exhibits convergence and irreversibility properties.
Model uncertainty consistently decreases over successive rounds of self-correction.
A strong dependence exists between the activated latent concept and model uncertainty, driving the convergence of self-correction performance.
papers.limitation:
The deeper algorithmic operations behind self-correction and the causal relationships between these operations and their associated behaviors are not explored.
The analysis focuses primarily on moral self-correction; self-correction mechanisms in other tasks (e.g., code generation, summarization) are not explored.
future_direction: External Feedback for Self-Correction: figuring out the performance upper bound of intrinsic self-correction to efficiently leverage external feedback.
Instruction Optimization: using the activated concept as a supervision signal to search for effective instructions.
The Connection between In-context Learning and Self-correction: exploring how in-context learning helps the emergence of self-correction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are able to improve their responses when instructed to do so, a capability known as self-correction. When instructions provide only a general and abstract goal without specific details about potential issues in the response, LLMs must rely on their internal knowledge to improve response quality, a process referred to as intrinsic self-correction. The empirical success of intrinsic self-correction is evident in various applications, but how and why it is effective remains unknown. Focusing on moral self-correction in LLMs, we reveal a key characteristic of intrinsic self-correction: performance convergence through multi-round interactions; and provide a mechanistic analysis of this convergence behavior. Based on our experimental results and analysis, we uncover the underlying mechanism of convergence: consistently injected self-correction instructions activate moral concepts that reduce model uncertainty, leading to converged performance as the activated moral concepts stabilize over successive rounds. This paper demonstrates the strong potential of moral self-correction by showing that it exhibits a desirable property of converged performance.

papers.title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does self-repair exist across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution, and what are the mechanisms behind it?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that self-repair exists across model families and sizes on the full pretraining distribution, and identifies two contributing mechanisms: changes in the LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing anti-erasure.
papers.conclusion: Self-repair is a real phenomenon that complicates interpretability efforts, and the findings provide evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis as a framework that predicts self-repair.
papers.key_findings:
Self-repair exists across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution.
Self-repair is imperfect and noisy, with the degree of compensation varying significantly across prompts.
A nontrivial fraction (around 30%) of self-repair can be attributed to changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor.
Sparse sets of neurons in MLP layers implement anti-erasure, contributing to self-repair, but the specific neurons vary across prompts.
Self-repair complicates interpretability efforts that rely on ablation-based metrics.
papers.limitation:
Self-repair is imperfect and noisy, making it difficult to quantify precisely.
Ablations take models off-distribution, leading to unpredictable and hard-to-interpret consequences.
future_direction: Control how far from distribution causal interventions take the model, e.g., by avoiding zero ablation or freezing LayerNorm.
Use path patching instead of patching full components to reduce off-distribution effects.
Further investigate the Iterative Inference hypothesis as an explanation for self-repair.
papers.abstract: Prior interpretability research studying narrow distributions has preliminarily identified self-repair, a phenomena where if components in large language models are ablated, later components will change their behavior to compensate. Our work builds off this past literature, demonstrating that self-repair exists on a variety of models families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution. We further show that on the full training distribution self-repair is imperfect, as the original direct effect of the head is not fully restored, and noisy, since the degree of self-repair varies significantly across different prompts (sometimes overcorrecting beyond the original effect). We highlight two different mechanisms that contribute to self-repair, including changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing Anti-Erasure. We additionally discuss the implications of these results for interpretability practitioners and close with a more speculative discussion on the mystery of why self-repair occurs in these models at all, highlighting evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis in language models, a framework that predicts self-repair.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
